questions.explanation:
Euler's relation: \(e^{jx}=\cos x+j\ \sin x\). The point \(e^{jx}\) sits on the unit circle at angle x.
• \(\cos x-j\ \sin x\) equals \(e^{-jx}\), the conjugate.
• \(\cos x+\sin x\) is a real number; it leaves out the j that puts \(\sin\) on the imaginary axis.
• An extra factor \(e^{x}\) would only appear if the exponent had a real part.

questions.prompt: For real x, what is the magnitude \(|e^{j\omega t}|\)?
questions.explanation: \(|e^{jx}|=\sqrt{\cos^{2}x+\sin^{2}x}=1\) for any real x. So \(e^{j\omega t}\) just rotates counter-clockwise around the unit circle at \(\omega\ \mathrm{rad}/\mathrm{s}\); its length never changes.

questions.prompt: What is the magnitude \(|z|\) of the complex number \(z=5-j12\)?
questions.explanation: \(|z|=\sqrt{\mathrm{Re}^2+\mathrm{Im}^2}=\sqrt{25+144}=\sqrt{169}=13\). The sign of the imaginary part does not matter for the magnitude. A common slip is adding the parts directly (\(5+12=17\)) or forgetting the square root (169).

questions.prompt: Find the phase angle of \(z=-2+j2\), in degrees (measured counter-clockwise from the positive real axis, between −180° and +180°).
questions.explanation:
z lies in the second quadrant (negative real part, positive imaginary part).
\(\tan^{-1}(y/x)=\tan^{-1}(2/(-2))=\tan^{-1}(-1)=-45^{\circ}\), but that calculator value points to the fourth quadrant. Add 180° to land in the correct quadrant: \(-45^{\circ}+180^{\circ}=135^{\circ}\).
Check: \(z=2\sqrt{2}\cdot e^{j135^{\circ}}=2.828(\cos 135^{\circ}+j\ \sin 135^{\circ})=-2+j2\checkmark\).

questions.prompt: Which expression correctly writes \(\cos(\omega t)\) using complex exponentials?
questions.explanation:
From Euler: \(e^{j\omega t}=\cos \omega t+j\ \sin \omega t\) and \(e^{-j\omega t}=\cos \omega t-j\ \sin \omega t\). Adding, the sines cancel: \(e^{j\omega t}+e^{-j\omega t}=2\cos \omega t\), so \(\cos \omega t=(e^{j\omega t}+e^{-j\omega t})/2\).
• Without the /2 you would have \(2\cos \omega t\).
• \((e^{j\omega t}-e^{-j\omega t})/(2j)\) is \(\sin \omega t\ (Eq\). 1.33).
• \((e^{j\omega t}-e^{-j\omega t})/2\) equals \(j\ \sin \omega t\), purely imaginary.

questions.prompt: Evaluate \(\mathrm{Re}\{(2\angle 30^{\circ})(3\angle 60^{\circ})/(1.5\angle-45^{\circ})\}\), where each number is written as magnitude∠angle.
questions.explanation:
Multiply magnitudes and add angles in the numerator; divide magnitudes and subtract angles for the quotient.
Magnitude: \((2\cdot 3)/1.5=4\). Angle: \(30^{\circ}+60^{\circ}-(-45^{\circ})=135^{\circ}\).
Result: \(4\angle 135^{\circ}=4\cos 135^{\circ}+j\cdot 4\ \sin 135^{\circ}\). Real part \(=4\cdot(-0.7071)=-2.828\).
Common mistake: subtracting the −45° incorrectly \((30^{\circ}+60^{\circ}-45^{\circ}=45^{\circ})\), which would give +2.83.

questions.prompt: Which of these complex exponentials has a real part equal to \(\sin(\omega t)\)?
questions.explanation:
\(\mathrm{Re}\{e^{j(\omega t-90^{\circ})}\}=\cos(\omega t-90^{\circ})=\sin(\omega t)\checkmark\).
• \(\mathrm{Re}\{e^{j(\omega t+90^{\circ})}\}=\cos(\omega t+90^{\circ})=-\sin(\omega t)\): wrong sign.
• \(j\cdot e^{j\omega t}=j\ \cos \omega t-\sin \omega t\), so \(\mathrm{Re}=-\sin(\omega t)\): wrong sign again.
• \(\mathrm{Re}\{e^{j\omega t}\}=\cos(\omega t)\), not \(\sin\).
Rule: \(\sin(\omega t)\) is \(\cos(\omega t)\) delayed by 90°, i.e., the phase is −90°.

questions.prompt: A student computes the product of two real signals \(x(t)=\cos(\omega t)\) and \(y(t)=\cos(\omega t+\phi)\) by multiplying their complex exponentials: '\(x\cdot y=\mathrm{Re}\{e^{j\omega t}\cdot e^{j(\omega t+\phi)}\}=\cos(2\omega t+\phi)\)'. What is wrong?
options: Nothing is wrong: the product of two cosines is \(\cos(2\omega t+\phi)\)
The result should be \(\cos(\phi)\), with no time dependence at all
The Re{ } trick only works for linear operations; the true product is \(\tfrac{1}{2}\cos \phi+\tfrac{1}{2}\cos(2\omega t+\phi)\), which includes a constant (DC) term
The result should be \(\tfrac{1}{2}\cos(2\omega t+\phi)\), because of the \(\tfrac{1}{2}\) in Euler's formula
questions.explanation:
Taking the real part commutes with linear operations (scaling, adding, differentiating, integrating), but NOT with multiplication: \(\mathrm{Re}\{ab\}\ne\mathrm{Re}\{a\}\cdot\mathrm{Re}\{b\}\).
Correct product: \(\cos(\omega t)\cos(\omega t+\phi)=\tfrac{1}{2}[\cos \phi+\cos(2\omega t+\phi)]\). Check at \(\phi=0\): \(\cos^{2}(\omega t)=\tfrac{1}{2}+\tfrac{1}{2}\cos(2\omega t)\checkmark\), which has an average value of \(\tfrac{1}{2}\).
• \(\cos(2\omega t+\phi)\) alone loses the constant term \(\tfrac{1}{2}\cos \phi\).
• \(\cos \phi\) alone loses the \(2\omega\) term and the \(\tfrac{1}{2}\) factors.
• \(\tfrac{1}{2}\cos(2\omega t+\phi)\) also loses the constant term.
This is why power (a product of v and i) needs care, as you will see in AC power.

questions.prompt: A decaying oscillation is written as the complex exponential \(v(t)=5\cdot e^{(-0.5+j10)t}\), with t in seconds. What is |v(t)| at \(t=2\ \mathrm{s}\)?
questions.explanation:
Split the exponent: \(e^{(-0.5+j10)t}=e^{-0.5t}\cdot e^{j10t}\). The factor \(e^{j10t}\) has magnitude 1, but \(e^{-0.5t}\) is a REAL exponential and does shrink.
\(|v(2)|=5\cdot e^{-0.5\cdot 2}\cdot 1=5e^{-1}=1.839\).
Common mistake: saying 'the magnitude of a complex exponential is always 1' and answering 5; that rule holds only for a purely imaginary exponent.
questions.figure_alt: A cosine oscillation inside a dashed exponentially decaying envelope starting at 5.

questions.prompt: Preview of sinusoidal steady state. A later skill says that for the input \(2\cos(\omega t)=\mathrm{Re}\{2e^{j\omega t}\}\), an LTI system with frequency response \(H=0.6-j0.3\) produces the output \(\mathrm{Re}\{2H\cdot e^{j\omega t}\}\). Write this output as \(A\cdot\cos(\omega t+\theta)\).
questions.explanation:
Write H in polar form: \(|H|=\sqrt{0.6^{2}+0.3^{2}}=0.6708\), and \(\angle H=\tan^{-1}(-0.3/0.6)=-26.57^{\circ}\) (fourth quadrant, so negative).
Then \(2H\cdot e^{j\omega t}=2\cdot 0.6708\cdot e^{j(\omega t-26.57^{\circ})}\), and the real part is \(1.342\cos(\omega t-26.57^{\circ})\).
• A + sign on the angle mistakes the sign of the imaginary part.
• 1.8 comes from adding the real and imaginary parts \((2\cdot(0.6+0.3))\), but magnitudes of complex numbers combine as \(\sqrt{a^{2}+b^{2}}\).
• −63.43° uses \(\tan^{-1}(0.6/0.3)\), swapping real and imaginary parts.

questions.prompt: Preview of poles and zeros. A response contains the term \(e^{st}\) with \(s=-2+j6\) (t in seconds). What is the magnitude \(|e^{st}|\) at \(t=0.4\ \mathrm{s}\)?
questions.explanation:
\(e^{st}=e^{-2t}e^{j6t}\). The factor \(e^{j6t}\) always has magnitude 1, so only the real part of s shrinks the term: \(|e^{st}|=e^{-2(0.4)}=e^{-0.8}=0.449\). Later, the real part of a pole sets how fast its term decays and the imaginary part sets how fast it oscillates.
• Answering 1 assumes every complex exponential has unit magnitude; that is only true when the exponent is purely imaginary.
• Using \(|s|\) (about 6.32) in the exponent mixes the oscillation rate into the decay.
questions.figure_alt: Real part of e^(st) for s = -2 + j6: a cosine oscillation inside a dashed exponentially decaying envelope.

questions.prompt: Preview of sinusoidal steady state. An LTI system has \(H=-0.4+j0.3\) at the input frequency, so the input \(5\cos(\omega t)\) produces \(\mathrm{Re}\{5He^{j\omega t}\}=2.5\cos(\omega t+\theta)\). What is \(\theta\) in degrees (between −180° and 180°)?
questions.explanation:
\(\theta=\angle H\). H has a negative real part and a positive imaginary part, so it lies in the second quadrant: \(\theta=180^\circ-\tan^{-1}(0.3/0.4)=180^\circ-36.87^\circ=143.13^\circ\). The magnitude checks out too: \(|H|=0.5\), so the amplitude is \(5\times0.5=2.5\).
• \(\tan^{-1}(0.3/-0.4)=-36.87^\circ\) is what a calculator's plain arctan returns; it points into the fourth quadrant, the wrong place.
• 36.87° drops the sign of the real part entirely.
